chapter_theme: The invocation goes for refuge to the god of gods, whose bliss is self-won and whose qualities never cease, and to his dharma and assembly; the poet asks the learned to wash his flaws as one washes a gem and to accept his words for their true matter, then begins the patikam's summary of Civakan's story: Saccandan's fall through desire and deafness to counsel, Vijayai's flight to the burning ground, Civakan's birth, learning, first victories, the powder contest of Suramanjari and Gunamalai, the dying dog, and the god who rescues him from prison.

the merchant who takes up and raises the newborn Civakan
the deceitful hunters whose seized herd Civakan frees
daughter of the Vidyadhara king, defeated by Civakan at the vina
a merchant's daughter who loses the scented-powder contest and shuns men

the god, once the dying dog Civakan helped, who carries him out of prison

1.reading: The poet goes for refuge to the red feet of the god of gods, whom the three worlds praise as the ageless First, and who is said to have reached by himself the supreme bliss that does not fail and to stand rich in qualities that never cease.
1.nuance: The god is defined by what he attained, not by what he made: தன்னின் எய்தி (reached it by himself) makes the bliss self-won, and the qualities (குணம்) are his wealth (நிதிச் செல்வன்). That this is the Jain Arhat is not said in the verse; the school tag rests on these marks and on the 1008 marks of verse 2. மூவா முதலா can be heard as 'the ageless First' or as two negatives, 'unaging, beginningless'; the claim does not turn on it.

claims.claim: the god of gods reached the highest unfailing bliss by his own effort and abides in unceasing qualities

2.reading: The poet places on his head the lotus feet, set on the golden crowns of the gods, of the holy form that blazes brighter than flame and bears the thousand and eight auspicious marks like green-gold letters written on a mountain of red gold.
2.nuance: The 1008 (ஆயிரத்து எட்டு) are marks on the body (மறு), not names; the simile makes the body a golden mountain and the marks an inscription on it. The gods' crowns carry the feet before the poet's head does, so the poet's gesture repeats theirs.

3.reading: The poet says he has gained a good excellence by going for refuge to the one who is the home of many qualities and has neither enmity nor friendship, to the ancient adorned dharma he stood in, and to the assembly of excellent word, and so has gained the excellence of setting down this work.
3.nuance: The verse goes to refuge in three: the teacher, his dharma, and the assembly (குழு). The threefold refuge is shared by Jain and Buddhist practice, and nothing in the verse decides between them; it is left without a school claim. பகை நண்பொடு இல்லான் makes the god's mark an absence of partiality, not a power to save. The refuge is given as the ground of the poet's right to compose (நாட்டுதல்).
3.event: The poet goes for refuge to the teacher, his dharma and the assembly before he begins.

4.reading: As even a gem thrown up by rock loses its fine quality if left unwashed, so the learned should wash with their wit the flaw thrown up in speech that is full like the bright white moon, and take the work set as an ornament.
4.nuance: மதி is used twice: வெண்மதி (the moon) and மதியால் (with the intellect), so the moon that carries a spot and the mind that cleans it share one word. The poet does not deny the flaw; he hands its removal to the reader, as a jeweller's duty.

5.reading: If coral, conch and pearl born in the sea taste of its salt, who would cast them away for that; so those who hold that one enters heaven through matter that is not false will accept the poet's words though they are faulty.
5.nuance: The apology moves from verse 4's ornament to substance: the worth of the work lies in its பொருள் (matter), as the worth of a pearl lies in itself and not in the brine it came from. The heaven claim is the readers' maxim, which the poet turns into a reason to accept him.

claims.claim: one reaches heaven by a teaching whose substance is true, so its faults of diction do not lessen it

6.reading: The poet announces his subject: Civakasami, a bull among men in the glory of having defeated the king who raised the fish banner, whose fame reached the sky, and whose story he has set out to tell to the assembly of the discerning as they stand with honey welling up.
6.nuance: மீன் ஏறு உயர்த்த கொடி வேந்தன, the king of the raised fish banner, is the Pandya's emblem, but the fish banner is also the god of love's; if the second is meant, the hero's glory is the conquest of desire that his final renunciation completes. The verse does not settle which, and the reading here keeps both.
6.event: Civakan defeats the king of the fish banner.

7.reading: The patikam opens the story on King Saccandan, of the unbending sceptre, the cool white umbrella, the army that never turns, the thunder-voiced elephants and victory that does not fade, and his queen Vijayai, whose chastity never gives way.
7.nuance: The king's praise is all outward power and the sceptre is called கோடாத (unbending); the queen's single epithet is வீடாத கற்பு. The next two verses show the king falling through his own desire while the queen's karpu is never in question.

8.reading: Vijayai, with eyes like a red lotus in full bloom, the grace of a green-gold creeper and a softness like nectar, became the king's nectar and the cause of his play.
8.nuance: ஏது (cause) is the hinge: her beauty is not blamed, but it is named as the cause of the king's pleasure, which verse 9 turns into the cause of his fall.

9.reading: The summary tells how the king, his desire grown dense and hard, would not hear the counsel offered and was beaten by a plot, and how, while his enemies rejoiced, the queen escaped on the mechanical peacock, lost her way and came down at the burning ground.
9.nuance: The cause given is the king's own: காமம் கனைந்து கன்றி and சொல்லாறு கேளான். Neither fate nor a former deed is named here, so the fall is told as a fault of rule, not as karma. The queen's flight ends at a burning ground (சுடுகாடு), where the hero will be born.
9.event: Saccandan, deaf to counsel in his desire, is overthrown by a plot, and Vijayai flees on the mechanical peacock to the burning ground.

10.reading: It goes on to tell how on the fated day the prince was born and the ten directions flourished, how a deity stood at the mother's shoulder as companion and ended her distress, how one took him up and reared him like a king who has gained a treasure, and how the sword-eyed mother kept a vow that her son might live.
10.nuance: நோற்ற is the verb of the vow: the mother does not stay to rear the child but turns to an ascetic discipline on his behalf. கோள் உற்ற கோன் போல் is hard: 'like a king who has seized a prize' fits the finder's joy, but the phrase may be corrupt or carry another sense.
10.event: Civakan is born at the burning ground, a deity relieves Vijayai, a foster father takes him to rear, and Vijayai takes a vow for her son.

11.reading: It tells how he swam the great sea of learning with his heart as raft, how the liberal one freed the herd taken by deceitful hunters, how the Vidyadhara king's daughter was defeated at the vina, and how he enjoyed among the townsmen a desire that carries poison.
11.nuance: நஞ்சு உற்ற காம places a judgment inside the summary: the pleasures the following books narrate at length are called poisoned before they begin. நாகர் may be the townspeople or the Naga folk; the reading takes the first.
11.event: Civakan masters the arts, frees the stolen herd from the hunters and defeats Gandharvadattai at the vina.

12.reading: It tells how, at the festival bath of the old city with conches crying and drums sounding, two dark-eyed young women fell into rivalry over their scented powder and said they would not bathe in this water if they had lost.
12.event: Suramanjari and Gunamalai wager on their scented powders at the festival bath.

13.reading: It tells how Suramanjari, her powder beaten, drooped, reviled Gunamalai, turned away smouldering like a wound struck again, resolved to look on no male form, and withdrew into the guarded mansion.
13.nuance: Her refusal to see any man is a vow of injured pride, not of renunciation; the patikam sets it up here to be undone in her own ilampakam.
13.event: Suramanjari loses the powder contest, abuses Gunamalai and shuts herself away from the sight of men.

14.reading: It tells how the gold-chested hero gave nectar to a dog that had come to harm at the bathing festival and stood dying, and how that same day he overcame the victorious elephant that had terrified Gunamalai.
14.nuance: புன்கண் எய்தி நின்று எஞ்சுகின்ற qualifies the dog (ஞமலி): it is the animal that came to grief at the festival bath, not the hero. அமிர்து here is not food: in the story it is the sacred formula whispered to the dying animal, and the verse's word lets the gift be both a mercy and a teaching. The pairing of the dog and the elephant on one day sets a kindness to the weakest beside a feat against the strongest.
14.event: Civakan gives the dying dog the nectar of the formula and the same day subdues the elephant that frightened Gunamalai.

15.reading: It tells how he won Gunamalai of honeyed speech, how the king, meaning him harm, seized him into prison, and how a god came down the sky's path like lightning from a cloud and carried the strong one of the flesh-scented spear away.
15.nuance: The verse does not say who the god is; in the story he is the dog of verse 14, reborn as a god, and the patikam's order sets the kindness and the rescue one verse apart. ஒளத in line 4 is not a word as printed.
15.event: Civakan marries Gunamalai, is imprisoned by the usurping king and is carried off by a god who descends from the sky.

links.note: Both name the Jain god by his qualities: the Cintamani's ஓவாது நின்ற குணத்து and தேவாதி தேவன், the Charana's litany with குணவதன், குணப்பெருங் கோமான், தேவன், and also சங்கரன் ஈசன் சயம்பு.
links.teaches: The Silappathikaram's Charana absorbs Saiva and Vedic titles into the Arhat's praise, while the Cintamani's invocation keeps to self-won bliss and qualities, so two Jain epics show two strategies, inclusive litany and bare definition.

links.note: The thousand and eight and the feet on the head recur: Kavunthi will speak only the ஆயிரத்து எட்டு நாமம் and bear only the flower feet on her head; the Cintamani's god bears ஆயிரத்து எட்டு marks and the poet sets his lotus feet on his head.
links.teaches: The number 1008 is a fixed token of Arhat worship that one epic attaches to names spoken and the other to marks on the body, while the feet-on-the-head gesture stays the same in a nun's vow and a poet's invocation.

links.note: Both apologies use the moon's spot for the poet's flaw: the Neelakesi's poet will own a fault since even the moon is not spotless; the Cintamani's asks the learned to wash the spot away with their wit.
links.teaches: The two Jain poets put the same flaw in different hands: the Neelakesi's poet takes it on himself, while the Cintamani's poet makes cleaning it the learned reader's task.

links.note: The Kural uses the spot on the moon to say a fault in the well-born is seen from far; the Cintamani uses it for a fault in a moon-full work and asks readers to wash it, not to see it.
links.teaches: The Kural's moon makes height expose a fault, but the Cintamani turns the same image into a reader's duty of charity, so the exposure the Kural warns of becomes something the audience may decline.

gains.a: the poet's request is seen to answer the expectation, stated in the Kural, that a high thing's fault draws every eye
gains.b: the couplet's warning is shown to depend on the onlooker, who can be asked to clean rather than point

links.note: Both prize what brackish ground or brine produces: the Naladiyar's salt above rice from good fields, the Cintamani's coral, conch and pearl though they taste of the sea.
links.teaches: The Naladiyar argues that a person's low origin does not lower his learning, and the Cintamani applies the same reasoning to a poem's faulty diction, so the brine image carries one argument about worth and origin from persons to texts.

gains.a: the apology is seen resting on an argument the ethics books had already made about rank
gains.b: the quatrain's claim about birth is shown extending to the standing of a work and its words

links.note: Verse 7 praises Saccandan's கோடாத செங்கோல் and unfading victory; verse 9 has the same king, sunk in desire and deaf to counsel, lose the kingdom to a plot.
links.teaches: The patikam builds the epic's first lesson from its own praise: the unbending sceptre and unfading victory are undone not by a stronger enemy but by the king's private desire.

links.note: The Kural says a king with no one to rebuke him perishes though he has no enemy; Saccandan had counsel (சொல்லாறு) and would not hear it.
links.teaches: The Cintamani's king shows that having rebuking counsellors is not enough, since desire can make a king deaf to them, so the Kural's safeguard fails at the point of hearing rather than of supply.

gains.a: the king's fall is given a named failure of rule, not only a lover's weakness
gains.b: the couplet's guard is shown to need a king who listens, which the couplet takes for granted

links.note: The Kural says those who set their desire on the home do not reach the fine fruit; the Cintamani's whole frame begins with a king whose desire for his queen grew thick and cost him his throne.
links.teaches: Held against the Kural's warning about desire fixed on the wife, the patikam locates the whole fault in the husband's excess while calling the queen's chastity unfailing (வீடாத கற்பு), and gives the couplet's lost 'fine fruit' a political price, the kingdom itself.

gains.a: the king's fall, told without any doctrine named, gains the Kural's category of being led by desire for the wife as its ethical name
gains.b: the couplet's unnamed 'fine fruit' is given a concrete price: a throne and, in the story, a life

links.note: The nectar given to the dying dog in verse 14 and the god who comes down to carry Civakan out of prison in verse 15 are, in the story, one being.
links.teaches: The patikam sets a small mercy and a great rescue one verse apart without naming their link, so the reader learns the epic's working of deeds by noticing that the rescuer is the dog.

links.note: The Kural weighs help given at the moment of need as greater than the world; Civakan's gift comes at a dying dog's last moment and is repaid by a god at his own.
links.teaches: The Kural measures timely help by its worth to the one helped, while the Cintamani shows it returned across species and births, so the couplet's weight becomes a debt that the receiver carries into a new life.

gains.a: the dog episode gains the Kural's measure of why so small a gift counts
gains.b: the couplet's timely help is shown being repaid in kind at the giver's own hour of need

new_concepts.gloss: the vow; a religious observance or discipline undertaken

source_issues: Verse 15 line 4: ஒளத (ஊன் நாறு ஒளத வேல்) is not a Tamil word as printed; a letter is likely lost or misread (perhaps ஔ split into ஒ+ள).
Verse 10 line 3: கோள் உற்ற கோன் போல் is hard to construe and may be corrupt.
Cast id for Civakan's father differs across this book's chapter files (saccandan in ch008, sachchandan in ch009); this chapter uses saccandan.
Cast id for the usurping minister also differs across this book's chapter files (kattiyangaran in ch011, kattiyankaran in ch010 and ch012); this chapter uses kattiyangaran.
